876.title: John of the Cross in prison
876.hook: imprisoned by his own brothers, he writes poems of love in a tiny cell, then escapes
876.howItsDone: Catholics honor John of the Cross as a saint and a Doctor of the Church; Carmelites and others read his poems and his writing on the dark night, and Christians of different churches turn to them in seasons when prayer feels empty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's small, poor, joyful houses. Your line was let nothing disturb you.

The cell is tiny, tradition says, little more than a closet, with light only from a narrow opening high in the wall. The man inside is a small, quiet friar who has been helping Teresa's reform among the men of her order. One night, friars of his own order who opposed the reform came and took him. Now they keep him locked in this cell in Toledo. He is brought out to be scolded, and, accounts say, beaten. Little light, almost nothing to read, the same clothes day after day. And in the dark he starts composing love poems in his head, memorizing them, since there's nothing to write with.

Later, the story goes, a kinder jailer gave him a little paper and ink, and he wrote some of the poems down. Then one night he got out through a high window and slipped away to a convent of Teresa's nuns, who hid him. Much of what he wrote is love poetry. Some hear an echo of the Song of Songs, where the beloved goes searching at night. In the King James Bible: "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth." One of his poems begins, in Spanish, en una noche oscura: on a dark night. A soul slips out of a quiet house, unseen, with no light to guide it except the one burning in the heart, and goes to meet the beloved. Scholars debate which poems were made in that cell. But the shape of the prison is in them: darkness, escape, a night that turns out to be the way to love. Later he wrote long explanations of the poem, and from them comes the idea behind a phrase people still use: the dark night of the soul. In ordinary speech it means a terrible stretch. For John it's more. It's a time when the usual lights go out, prayer feels empty, and God, he says, is working in the dark where we can't see. A psalm says: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." The friar in the closet wrote love songs with almost no light.

Let something hard come to mind, in your life or the world, without fixing it. Then look gently for one beautiful thing beside it, a kindness, a face, a small mercy, and shape it into one line of a poem, kept in your head the way John did. If you pray, offer the line to God; if you don't, let it sit beside the hard thing.

Your line: on a dark night. Even the dark can hold a love song. See you tomorrow.

877.title: Philip Neri
877.hook: the laughing saint of Rome, who wore his clothes inside out to stay humble
877.howItsDone: Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the Oratory communities that look back to him still gather for prayer, scripture and music; stories of his humor are often retold on his feast day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, noche oscura: John of the Cross, writing love poems in a tiny cell. Your line was on a dark night.

A priest is walking through the streets of Rome with half his beard shaved off. Another day, tradition says, he goes out with his clothes on inside out. People stare. Some laugh. That's the point. This is Philip Neri, and Rome remembers him as the laughing saint. People came to him for confession and advice, and some hoped to meet a holy man. What they found, the stories say, might be a joke, a silly hat, or a book of funny stories read aloud with a perfectly straight face. Behind it all sat a serious question: how do you stay humble when people start calling you a saint?

He lived in Rome in the age of the reformations, when the Catholic Church was working to renew itself from the inside. He didn't lead armies of preachers or write a famous book. He talked with people and heard confessions. He gathered young men in a room to pray, read scripture, sing and talk about God, and the community that grew from those meetings came to be called the Oratory. Tradition says that when people began treating him as a living saint, he'd do something ridiculous on purpose, so they'd laugh at him instead of praising him. He wasn't mocking holiness. He was guarding it. The saying linked to him is today's line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart. It echoes a proverb in the King James Bible: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones." And Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, says of giving: "for God loveth a cheerful giver." Seen this way, cheerfulness isn't a mood that shows up when life is easy. It's a strength you can lean on. A heart that can laugh at itself is harder to puff up, and harder to crush. And if you don't need to look impressive, your attention is free to go to other people. Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the proverb he echoes sits in the Bible Christians share.

Do one small, humbly silly thing, never at anyone else's expense: hum a tune badly, or read a line aloud in a ridiculous voice, and let yourself smile. Notice the little voice asking what people would think, and breathe until it gets a little smaller. If you pray, hold the proverb gently: a merry heart doeth good like a medicine. If not, rest in the lightness of not having to look impressive.

Your line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart. Even a saint can wear his clothes inside out. I'm glad you came.

878.title: Francis de Sales
878.hook: a gentle bishop: nothing is so strong as gentleness
878.tomorrow: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac
878.howItsDone: Catholics honor Francis de Sales as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and his Introduction to the Devout Life is still read by Christians of different churches as a guide to prayer in ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip Neri, the laughing saint with half a beard. Your line was cheerfulness strengthens the heart.

"A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." That's a proverb in the King James Bible, and it sounds easy until someone is shouting. Then the grievous words come quickly. Today's figure is a bishop who, tradition says, had a hot temper by nature, and spent his life learning the soft answer instead. People came to call him the gentleman saint. A saying linked to his name goes something like this: nothing is so strong as gentleness, and nothing so gentle as real strength.

Francis de Sales was a Catholic priest, then a bishop, when Catholics and Protestants in his corner of Europe were deeply divided. Tradition says that as a young priest he was sent into a region that had become Protestant, and when people wouldn't come to hear him, he wrote short pages explaining his faith and slipped them under doors. Whatever you make of his arguments, notice the method: patient, quiet, personal. He wrote a book called Introduction to the Devout Life, as letters of advice to a woman living an ordinary life in the world. Its big idea: a life of prayer isn't only for monks and nuns. A soldier, a shopkeeper, a parent, a servant can each be devout in the life they already have. And the way there, again and again in his writing, is gentleness, with others and with yourself. When you fall short, he advises, don't rage at yourself. Pick yourself up the way you'd lift a friend who tripped. Harshness, in his view, just adds a second problem to the first. Paul lists gentleness among the fruit of the Spirit: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith". And in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus describes himself this way: "for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls." Gentleness here isn't weakness. It's strength that has decided not to crush.
screen: `A DEVOUT LIFE, RIGHT WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: Think of a hard conversation coming up, or one that keeps replaying, and let the other person's sharpest line arrive; notice where it lands, in the jaw, the chest, the hands. Breathe out slowly, and silently try one soft answer: not a surrender, just a sentence with no edge on it. If you pray, hold the proverb as you breathe: a soft answer turneth away wrath. If not, stay with the slower breath and the unclenched jaw.
Gentleman saint. The nickname for Francis de Sales, the bishop who taught that gentleness, with others and with yourself, is a kind of strength.
Your line: nothing so strong as gentleness. That goes for how you treat yourself, too. Day eight hundred seventy-eight, done.

879.title: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac
879.hook: a priest and a widow organize charity for the poor of Paris
879.howItsDone: Catholics honor Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac as saints; the Daughters of Charity and the lay Society of Saint Vincent de Paul carry on their work, and parish groups named for him run visits and food pantries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales, the gentleman saint. Your line was nothing so strong as gentleness.

One Sunday in a French country parish, just before the sermon, the priest hears that a whole family nearby is sick, with no one to look after them. He tells the congregation. That afternoon, the story goes, people stream down the road with soup, bread and blankets. Too much, all at once. Some of the food goes to waste, and by next week the family could be alone again. Kindness had shown up, but nobody had organized it. So the priest writes a simple plan: who goes on which day, what they bring, how they speak to the sick. That priest was Vincent de Paul.

The plan grew. Groups of women in parish after parish took turns visiting the sick poor, and Vincent needed someone to hold it all together. He found her in Louise de Marillac, a widow with a sharp mind and, tradition says, a long struggle with anxiety and doubt of her own. She traveled to the groups, checked on them, trained them, and wrote to Vincent about what was working. Together they gathered young women into a community that came to be called the Daughters of Charity. They were not to live behind convent walls, but out among people: in hospitals, in homes, with orphans, in the streets of Paris. Vincent is remembered for putting it this way: their cloister would be the streets of the city. The reason sits in Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus says: "I was sick, and ye visited me". And then: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Today's line is linked to Vincent too: the poor are our masters. It flips the usual picture. The helper isn't the one in charge. The people being served are the ones to be honored, listened to and waited on, the way a good servant attends to a household. Catholics honor both as saints, and the Daughters of Charity still serve today.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Think of who near you needs help: a food bank, a shelter, a sick neighbor, someone at a care home who rarely gets visitors. Pick one, and do what Vincent did: make it concrete, which day, what time, what you'd bring. Then let the plan go and breathe; if you pray, rest with the words I was sick, and ye visited me, and if not, with the face of the person you'd serve.
Vincent. The priest who turned scattered kindness into organized care for the poor of Paris, working with Louise de Marillac to send women out to serve in the streets.
Your line: the poor are our masters. Kindness, given a plan. That's day eight hundred seventy-nine.

880.title: St Bartholomew's Day (1572)
880.hook: Protestants killed in Paris; religion used for massacre
880.howItsDone: Christians of different churches remember the massacre in histories, sermons and services of repentance and reconciliation, and pray for places where religion is used to justify violence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac, turning scattered kindness into a plan. Your line was the poor are our masters.

It begins with a wedding. In Paris, the Catholic king's sister marries the Protestant king of Navarre, a match meant to help end years of fighting between French Catholics and French Protestants, who were called Huguenots. Protestant nobles come to the city to celebrate. Soon after, on the feast of the apostle Bartholomew, the killing starts. First the Huguenot leaders. Then neighbors turn on neighbors in the streets, and the violence spreads to other towns. A day on the church calendar, named for one of the twelve, becomes the name of a massacre. This is a hard lesson, and an honest one.

Historians still argue about who gave the orders, and how much was planned and how much was a mob let loose. What isn't in doubt: people were killed for their faith by people who said they shared the same Lord. In the wars of religion that tore at France, both Catholics and Protestants killed, and both were killed. St Bartholomew's Day is the one whose name stuck. And this exact temptation shows up in the Gospels. In Luke, a Samaritan village turns Jesus and his friends away. James and John ask if they should call down fire from heaven to destroy it. In the King James Bible: "But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of." And on the night of his arrest, when one of his followers draws a sword to defend him (John's Gospel names him as Peter), Jesus says, in Matthew: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." His own followers, reaching for violence on his behalf, and both times he says no. That's where today's line comes from: never in his name. It isn't a line about other people's faiths. It's one Christians can turn on their own story, honestly, without pretending it didn't happen. Remembering a day like this isn't about blame across the centuries. It's about recognizing the moment a faith starts to be used as a weapon, so the sword goes back in its place.
screen: `KILLED BY THOSE WHO SHARED THEIR LORD.`

Your line: never in his name. A hard day to remember, and worth remembering. Rest well.

881.title: The Thirty Years' War
881.hook: Europe tears itself apart until the Peace of Westphalia
881.howItsDone: Christians in different churches pray for places at war in their services and at home, and the beatitude 'blessed are the peacemakers' is one they may read when they do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Bartholomew's Day and the Huguenots, a wedding that ended in a massacre. Your line was never in his name.

In Prague, an angry crowd of Protestant nobles storms into a castle room, grabs royal officials, and throws them out of a high window. The officials survive the fall. The story goes that Catholics said angels had caught them, while their enemies said they'd landed in a heap of dung. Either way, nobody laughed for long. That window opened onto a war that would grind on and on across German lands: armies coming and going and coming back, Catholic and Protestant rulers on both sides, and plenty of soldiers fighting mainly for pay.

It started as a quarrel about religion and rights in Bohemia. It didn't stay there. Kings and princes joined in for faith, for land, for power, and the lines blurred: Catholic France ended up backing Protestant armies against the Catholic Habsburgs. The religious labels stayed on the banners, but the reasons kept multiplying. And the kings didn't pay. Villagers did, in the path of armies that lived off the land, taking food, burning farms, leaving hunger and sickness behind. Then, slowly, came the end. Diplomats gathered in two towns in Westphalia, in northwest Germany, Catholics in one and Protestants in the other, and the talks dragged on. Out of them came the Peace of Westphalia. It didn't make anyone agree about God. It set terms for living side by side: Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed rulers were all recognized, and Europe began, unevenly, to step back from fighting wars over which church was right. Peace at last, but a tired peace, bought at a terrible cost. The prophet Isaiah describes a different ending, in the King James Bible: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Westphalia wasn't that. Treaties never quite are. But it was a step back from the edge. And Jesus' words sit beside any peace table: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

Choose one place where fighting hasn't ended, and look for the people working to stop it: a negotiator at a long table, a medic, a neighbor sharing bread across a line. Breathe in and let one of them come close; breathe out and wish them strength for the slow work. If you pray, pray for them in your own words or rest with blessed are the peacemakers; if you don't, keep them in your attention and wish their place peace at last.
Westphalia. The peace treaty that ended the Thirty Years' War, letting Catholic and Protestant rulers live side by side without agreeing about God.
Your line: peace at last. A tired peace is still a peace. Day eight hundred eighty-one, done.

882.title: The King James Bible (1611)
882.hook: scholars working in companies produce an English Bible whose phrases are still in the language
882.carry: the language of heaven, in english
882.howItsDone: Some churches read the King James Version in every service, while others use newer translations and keep the King James for familiar passages such as Psalm 23, read at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Thirty Years' War, and a tired treaty in Westphalia. Your line was peace at last.

The salt of the earth. A law unto themselves. The powers that be. Fight the good fight. The skin of my teeth. People say these without a second thought, at work, in sports commentary, in arguments about politics. Every one sits, word for word, in the same old book. In the book of Job, a man who has lost nearly everything says: "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth." The book is an English Bible made at the order of a king, and its sound has hung around in the language ever since.

King James ruled England and Scotland when English Christians were reading more than one translation, and arguing about them. So a new one was ordered, to be read aloud in churches. Teams of scholars took different parts of the Bible, and their drafts were checked and revised together. The title page says it was translated out of the original tongues, with the former translations diligently compared and revised. That last part matters. The translators didn't start from nothing. They leaned on English Bibles that came before, including the work of William Tyndale, who had been executed as a heretic. Their preface to the reader uses a string of pictures for what translation does: it opens a window to let in the light, it breaks the shell so we can eat the kernel, it pulls back the curtain. And the result was made for the ear. Listen to the twenty-third Psalm: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters." Short words, a steady beat, made to be said out loud in a stone church. Some Christians still read the King James as their main Bible, and others treasure it alongside newer translations. Either way, its rhythm is why today's line fits: the language of heaven, in english.
screen: `A NEW TRANSLATION, ORDERED BY A KING.`
`A WINDOW TO LET IN THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Read Psalm twenty-three aloud, from a Bible or a phone if you have one, or just the lines from today: the LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. Read slowly, at a speaking volume, as if to a room, then sit with the sound still in the air. If you pray, let the psalm become your prayer; if you don't, notice the rhythm and what it does to your breath.
Tyndale. The earlier English Bible translator whose work the King James translators leaned on, though he had been executed as a heretic.
Your line: the language of heaven, in english. Old words, still in everyday mouths. That's day eight hundred eighty-two.
